---
title: "Quiz: medial axis and reconstruction"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $\mathrm{DT}(p)$ is the distance from an object pixel to the nearest background pixel.

---

**Q1.** In the grassfire picture, what does the time at which the fire reaches a point correspond to?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The fire moves inwards from the whole boundary at unit speed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Its distance to the nearest boundary point: the distance transform $\mathrm{DT}$. The skeleton is where fronts from different parts of the boundary arrive at the same time and meet.
:::

---

**Q2.** A disc inside a band touches only one side of the band. Why is it not maximal?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Can it move and grow?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It can slide away from that side and grow until it touches the other side as well; the bigger disc contains the first one. Only discs that touch the boundary in at least two places (or sit in a corner that fits them exactly) are maximal.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why can the shape be rebuilt exactly from its medial axis, but not from a thinning skeleton?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does each one store?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The medial axis stores the centres of all maximal discs with their radii, and every point of the shape lies in one of them: their union is the shape. A thinning skeleton is only approximately centred and does not reach into all corners, so the union of discs of radius $\mathrm{DT}$ on it misses some pixels (the corners, the tips of thin arms).
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does the medial axis of a rectangle fork at both ends when the discs are round (or diamonds), but not when they are squares?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the largest disc that fits into a corner?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A round disc pushed into a right-angled corner touches both sides at once: the small discs along the corner's diagonal are maximal, so the axis runs out to the corners. A square disc fits into the corner of a rectangle perfectly, and the square of the midline already covers the corner: no extra maximal discs, no fork.
:::

---

**Q5.** A one-pixel bump appears on the boundary of a smooth shape. What does it do to the medial axis, and why is that a problem for measuring?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does the bump have its own maximal discs?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The bump is touched by new maximal discs, and their centres form a whole new branch from the axis to the bump. A branch count or total length would change because of a single noisy pixel. The medial axis is not continuous in the shape: remedies are smoothing the mask, pruning short branches, or keeping only axis points whose nearest boundary points are far apart (λ).
:::

---

**Q6.** Lantuéjoul's formula uses only erosions, openings, differences and unions. Which pixels end up in $S_r$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the opening keep?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The pixels where a disc of radius $r$ (the element $B$ dilated $r$ times) fits, but which are not covered by any fitting disc of radius $r + 1$: the centres of the maximal discs of radius $r$. The opening keeps exactly the pixels covered by a bigger fitting disc, and the difference removes them.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Write the reconstruction of a shape from Lantuéjoul's sets $S_r$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each pixel of $S_r$ is the centre of a disc of radius $r$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$A = \bigcup_{r \ge 0} S_r \oplus rB$, with $rB$ the element $B$ dilated $r$ times (and $0B$ the origin). Each $S_r \oplus rB$ is the union of the maximal discs of radius $r$.
:::

---

**Q8.** For a vessel mask, what is $2\,\mathrm{DT}$ read on the skeleton?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What touches the vessel wall?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The local **diameter**: on the centreline the largest disc touches both walls, so its radius $\mathrm{DT}$ is half the width. Read along the skeleton, it gives a radius profile for each branch.
:::
